title: Rust: Simple Memory Allocator
description: Implement a simple bump allocator and free-list allocator in Rust.

steps.title: Bump Allocator
steps.description: Create a `BumpAllocator` that manages a fixed-size buffer `[u8; 1024]`. Implement `allocate(&mut self, size: usize) -> Option<*mut u8>` that returns a pointer and bumps the offset. Print allocations.
hints: `allocate`: if offset + size <= 1024, get pointer at offset, increment offset.
Return None if out of memory.

verification.failureMessage: Allocate memory and print the pointer addresses.

steps.title: Free List Allocator
steps.description: Implement a free-list allocator. When memory is freed, add it back to the free list. Use a linked list of free blocks stored inline. Test allocate + free + allocate again.
hints: Track free blocks as `Vec<(usize, usize)>` (offset, size).
On `free`, add the block back to the free list and merge adjacent blocks.
On `allocate`, find a free block large enough (first-fit).

verification.failureMessage: Allocate, free, and re-allocate to show memory reuse.

steps.title: Alignment Support
steps.description: Add alignment support: `allocate_aligned(&mut self, size: usize, align: usize) -> Option<*mut u8>`. Align the pointer to the specified boundary. Test with 4-byte and 8-byte alignment.
hints: Round up offset to the next aligned address.
Bump allocator with alignment is 90% of real malloc behavior.

verification.failureMessage: Allocate with 4-byte and 8-byte alignment and print addresses.

steps.title: Type-Safe Allocation
steps.description: Create a type-safe wrapper: `alloc<T>(&mut self, value: T) -> &mut T` that allocates space for T and writes the value. Also `dealloc<T>(&mut self, ptr: &mut T)`. Test with integers and strings.
hints: This is how custom allocators work in embedded systems.

verification.failureMessage: Allocate and use an i32 and String through the allocator.

steps.title: Memory Statistics
steps.description: Add statistics tracking: total allocated, total freed, current usage, peak usage, allocation count. Print a statistics report after a series of operations.
hints: Track stats: `bytes_allocated: usize, bytes_freed: usize, allocation_count: u32`
Print report: `println!("Used: {} bytes, Peak: {} bytes, Count: {}", ...)`
This is similar to what `/proc/meminfo` shows on Linux.
